premise.headline: A hero meets his worst emergency: applause.

featureImagePrompt:
Create one polished web feature image for Paperclipalypse.

ASPECT RATIO: exactly 2:1, horizontal wide banner.

This must be a clear illustrated comedy poster, not a busy comic page.

Layout:
- LEFT 40%: one clean full-color illustration. A charming anthropomorphic metallic paperclip stand-up comedian at a microphone on a small stage, with a simple diner scene behind him: one choking diner, one calm antisocial diner eating fries. Keep this side simple and uncluttered.
- RIGHT 60%: one flat dark charcoal poster panel with a bronze frame. This panel is mostly typography. Use large cream-white plain sans-serif lettering, like a clean printed poster, not distorted hand lettering.

TEXT ACCURACY IS THE TOP PRIORITY. The right poster panel must contain exactly these lines, with normal spaces between words:

I'm so antisocial that being a hero
is my worst nightmare.

A guy started choking at a diner.
I know the Heimlich maneuver,
and I'm fine with bruising a rib
to save him.

But if it works, he survives.
And if he survives, I have to make
awkward small talk while the whole
restaurant claps.

I kept eating my fries.
I figured he'd want his privacy.

Rules:
- Spell every word correctly.
- Do not merge words together.
- Do not invent letters.
- Keep the text entirely inside the right panel with generous margins.
- Do not add any other visible words, signs, captions, labels, logos, watermarks, signatures, or fake microtext anywhere else.
- If space is tight, make the illustration simpler and the right text panel larger. Do not remove, rewrite, or garble the text.

jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: Bedside Manner
jokes.joke: I have the bedside manner of an emergency room physician. My buddy started choking at dinner, so I did the Heimlich hard enough to crack a rib. He said, “You hurt me!” I said, “That’s how you know it’s working.” Now nobody asks me to open pickle jars.

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Portal to Healing
jokes.joke: I've been seeing a therapist for six months and I finally understand what she means by 'opening a portal to your inner child.' Last Tuesday I cried for forty minutes about a Capri Sun. Forty minutes. About the straw. About how I could never get the straw in. She called it a breakthrough. I called it seven dollars in parking.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: The Hero's Dilemma
jokes.joke: I'm so antisocial that being a hero is my worst nightmare. A guy started choking at a diner the other day. I know the Heimlich maneuver, and I'm completely fine with the concept of hurting someone to save them—bruise a rib, whatever. But if it works, he survives. And if he survives, I have to make awkward small talk while the whole restaurant claps. I just kept eating my fries. I figured he'd want his privacy.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: ER Tough Love
jokes.joke: Folks, I ended up in the ER after a stupid fall. The Emergency Room Physician looks at my messed-up shoulder and says, 'Sometimes you gotta hurt someone to save them.' Then he yanks it back into place. I'm screaming bloody murder and he just nods like, 'See? Working already.' Thanks, doc—I'm healed, but now I know why your job requires a poker face. You're all just professional hurters with better parking spots.

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Coping Skills
jokes.joke: I told my therapist I might be a little antisocial, and she said, “Try opening up to people.” So I did. I opened up to one guy in the waiting room, and he immediately switched seats. At this point I’m not antisocial—I’m just collecting data that everyone else agrees with my diagnosis.

scores.comment: Clear first-person bit with a specific childhood image and a solid final deflation; not huge, but well-shaped.
Strong antisocial-hero premise with a satisfying privacy turn; a bit long, but the comic logic is clear.
Understandable and stage-shaped, but it leans heavily on repeating the seed premise and the punchline is fairly expected.
Clean therapy-room joke with a neat final line; familiar territory, but the diagnosis/data turn works.
Clean escalation and the pickle jar button lands well. The 'that's how you know it's working' line is a satisfying turn, though the overall shape is familiar. Solid stage joke.

The inversion is genuinely fresh: avoiding heroism not out of cowardice but to dodge social obligation. 'I figured he'd want his privacy' is an excellent final line. The fries detail grounds it. One of the stronger angles in the batch.
Competent ER setup but the 'professional hurters with better parking spots' ending is more clever than funny. The punchline tries too hard and the poker face line is a detour. Respectable filler.

Tight and clean. 'Collecting data that everyone agrees with my diagnosis' reframes the premise neatly without being smug. The waiting room detail is concrete. Slightly predictable in shape but the final line earns it.
The premise is solid, but the final punchline about pickle jars feels structurally disconnected from the Heimlich maneuver setup.
Excellent stage rhythm and specific details. The escalation of the Capri Sun straw perfectly contrasts with the mundane reality of the parking fee punchline.
Feels too literal and anecdotal. The seed terms are recited clumsily, and the final punchline lacks comic snap.
Clean construction with a solid, logical turn at the end. The premise is relatable and well-executed with good economy of words.
Solid premise with strong final twist on pickle jars; natural delivery and good escalation.
Mild therapy absurdity with specific detail; relatable but follows expected inner-child trope.
Sharp ironic antisocial hero premise with clean, memorable punch on privacy; strong stage rhythm.
Competent waiting-room bit but predictable payoff; mild smile at best.
Solid premise with a clean turn; competent and mildly funny.
Good imagery and a relatable payoff; leans on familiar therapy beats but works.
Fresh angle on antisocial behavior with a strong final turn; the best of the batch.
Clear and competent but follows a predictable ER-shoulder-reset pattern.
